newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - Polish c.bank to tighten monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Polish c.bank to tighten monetary policy.

text.p: Poland's central bank chief Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Thursday the bank would further tighten monetary policy to offset inflationary effects of the ruling left's plans to relax fiscal discipline next year.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz told a news conference the government plan to keep the budget gap at 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, or 12 billion zlotys, instead of cutting it to 2.6 percent as earlier planned, would force the National Bank of Poland to step up its anti-inflationary efforts.
"There is a correlation between monetary and fiscal policies (and)... since fiscal discipline has been loosened, ours will have to be more restrictive," she said.
The government decided to widen the budget gap in order to offer a moderate tax cut next year.

But in a surprise vote on Thursday the lower house of parliament voted for an even deeper tax cut, which Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko estimated could cost about 4.5 billion zlotys in lost revenues, two billion more than the earlier planned tax cut.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said that the 2.8 percent deficit, coupled with this year's inflation topping the 17 percent plan, had already made next year's inflation target of 13 percent year-on-year unrealistic.

She said the bank, which earlier signalled it would allow real interest rates to rise to control fast growth of credit, was especially concerned over a rise in banking financing of the deficit, which might boost nominal market rates.
"It is possible that increased financing (of the deficit) in the banking system will boost money rates," she said.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz did not say how the decision by the lower house, to replace the planned 20, 31 and 43 percent tax rates with a four-level scale of 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent, would affect next year's inflation.
But she said the bank would adjust its instruments to meet its key monetary targets and keep inflation as low as possible.
She said the bank sought to keep broad money supply growth next year at 6.8-7.6 percent in real terms or 27.4 and 28.6 billion zlotys, against this year's 27 billion zloty growth plan.
It also set the key operating target of reserve money growth at between 5.2 and 7.5 billion zlotys.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the restrictive monetary policy would also require the pace of the crawling zloty devaluation to lag inflation and that the bank initially assumed the 1997 devaluation at nine percent, which meant strengthening of the currency in real terms.

She said that while such a pace of the zloty's gradual devaluation against a basket of currencies would have a deflationary effect, it would result in the registered trade deficit widening to $9.9 billion next year.
In August the gap stood at $4.5 billion.
As another measure aimed at controlling monetary expansion the bank would put off for some time its earlier plan to lower obligatory reserves for banks.
"For the time being, it (the deficit level) means that there will be no lowering (of obligatory reserves)," she said.
